subsubtopic: ALLEGED THEFT OF CHEESE IMPORT CERTIFICATES-DAIRY FARMERS' LOSSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government places a low priority on agriculture in Canada and on its importance to the Canadian economy. After the recent theft of Government import certificates for cheese the Government forced the importers using these certificates to pay a 10 per cent fine and return the illegally imported cheese to the country of origin. That may have been an appropriate action if there was no illegal action by the importers.
What is not appropriate and not fair is the treatment that has been handed out to Canadian dairy producers. They have been assessed over-quota levies of millions of dollars because some civil servant stole a bunch of import certificates and peddled them to make a fast buck. Why are these producers being fined by having this unfair levy imposed on them? The Minister's defence of the Government's action is as full of holes as Swiss cheese.
The Government should stop picking on the farmers and reimburse them for these levies which have been estimated by the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture Dairy Committee to be $5.6 million. The Tory caucus has known about this for six months. We need action from the Government now.

On Wednesday, Mr. Speaker, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation sold Habitat 67 to a speculator despite the fact that two-thirds of the tenants had made a bid for the entire housing complex.
Forming an association, 100-odd tenants offered close to $10 million. They stated that they wanted mainly to continue to live in their units and, "above all else we want Habitat 67 to
remain in its present conditions as part of our national heritage".
In its purchasing offer the tenants' association made a commitment to protect the existing structure and the exterior appearance of the building. It also asked CMHC management to give it an opportunity to make a counter-offer and the corporation had promised to negotiate with respect to the highest bids.
Just the same, CMHC sold the complex to a speculator for $10 million without giving the tenants an opportunity to defend their own interests.
This is most unfair on the part of this Conservative Government which as usual gives priority to the interests of speculators over those of tenants and workers.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF PACIFIC NATIVE FISHING ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to commend the Native Brotherhood of B.C. for their hard work in securing the position of native fishermen in the B.C. Fishing industry. I also want to commend the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) for providing $11 million to the Native Brotherhood of B.C. These moneys are to be administered by the newly formed Pacific Native Fishing Association which will operate under the auspices of the Native Brotherhood of B.C.
The Association will provide financial assistance to native fishing vessel owners, assist former operators of rental vessels such as the Cassiar Native Rental Fishermen to purchase their own boats, provide basic business management training, and ensure that native fishermen who wish to leave the industry pass their vessels and licences to other natives through a purchase plan managed by the new association.
Today the Minister announced the members of the board for the new fishing association. These members were selected by the executive of the Native Brotherhood of B.C. I want to extend my best wishes to the Native Brotherhood of B.C. as they meet today and tomorrow in Masset, B.C., for their annual convention.

November 29, 1985

subsubtopic: CANADA'S DECISION TO PARTICIPATE IN ESTABLISHING INTERNATIONAL AGENCY TO COMBAT TERRORISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, November 23, we watched, shocked and helpless, as a tragedy unfolded that was to end in the death of two Canadian citizens, innocent victims of an act of international terrorism in Malta. I am sure that this tragic accident has once more aroused in Canadians feelings of indignation and disgust at these thoughtless acts of terrorism, at a time when terrorism has become common as a form of protest, but at what price!
Despite the tragic outcome of this incident which aroused general consternation among the Canadian public, I would like to point out the excellent work done by officials of the Department of External Affairs, their speedy intervention, their close co-operation with the bereaved family and their sense of duty.
I am sure that Canadians were very pleased and vastly relieved at the announcement yesterday by Canada's ambassador to the United Nations that Canada has decided to help set up an international agency to combat terrorism. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this agency will be to defeat international terrorism, since no one can be entirely safe from its effects. We therefore have a duty to support the action taken by our Government, so that tragic events such as the Achille Lauro affair, the EgyptAir incident and the attack against the Turkish Embassy will never happen again.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PROGRAMS TO HELP LAID-OFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in Quebec, more than 500 community agencies set up a coalition to ask the Government, and more specifically, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), to review her decision on criteria for job development programs, which now make it compulsory for all futur employees in these programs to have been unemployed for 24 of the 30 last weeks. If the Government does not change its decision, it will mean that all those who have agreed to work under the Government's Canada Works program will be excluded from subsequent programs, and that if the Government maintains this attitude, community agencies in Quebec and the other provinces will have to close their doors.
Mr. Speaker, this particular coalition includes the Regrou-pement des maisons des jeunes du Quebec, the Association des centres de femmes du Quebec, the Mouvement d'action popu-laire et d'action communautaire du Quebec, the Association quebecoise pour la defense des droits des retraites et des preretraites, and the Confederation des organismes provinciaux pour personnes handicapees and various shelter facilities. All those agencies are asking the Government to remember that community agencies can do excellent work for the public while at the same time providing manpower training, provided they are allowed to hire people with experience.

subsubtopic: SINKING OF FISHING VESSEL LADY MARJORIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call to the attention of the House the sinking off the coast of Nova Scotia of the fishing vessel Lady Marjorie, by the Canadian Navy vessel H.M.C.S. Nipigon. The Navy will undoubtedly resolve the procedural problems internally to prevent a recurrence of this type of event in the future. However, the Conservative Government has a clear responsibility to compensate the owner of the vessel. The owner of the Lady Marjorie must be compensated for the loss of the vessel in such a negligent and dangerous manner.
In addition, the owner owned a small fish processing operation based on production from his vessel. That plant employed 15 people. As a result of the sinking of this vessel by the Navy, that plant is closed and 15 people are out of work.
The Minister of National Defence and Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) must act quickly on the matter. 1 also note that no member of the Conservative Party from Nova Scotia has seen fit up to this point to raise this important matter in the House of Commons and urge the Government to move quickly toward compensation. It is important that they join the NDP and speak up on behalf of the people whom they were elected to represent. The Government must provide compensation, and provide it quickly.

subsubtopic: CENTENNIAL CELEBRATIONS OF NIAGARA PARKS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1985 is the centennial of the Niagara Parks Commission and I would like to draw the attention of the House to some of the work the Commission is doing to promote tourism in Canada. Many people do not realize that the Commission is completely self-supporting and is run as a business. Moneys are raised through gift shops, restaurants, attractions, and through water rentals to power companies. Funds are used to maintain not only the lands and gardens but also the buildings and roadways. The Niagara Parks Commission has its own police force as well as 1,400 employees.
November 29, 1985

Last week the third annual winter Festival of Lights, an international light show that runs for three months, began. Along with the nightly illumination on the falls, 30,000 lights are strewn over 55 giant trees. Private companies have joined the celebration, making the winter Festival of Lights a real community celebration.
This Festival has resulted in an increase of over one million tourists visiting the Niagara area and has been an incredible boost for local merchants and business people. The Niagara Parks Commission is to be congratulated not only for its tremendous work over the last 100 years but for its continual leadership in the tourist industry.
As I mentioned yesterday when I presented a petition, there is tremendous potential for attracting tourists to Canada by way of the attractions of the Niagara Peninsula and we need to encourage this in any way we can, both federally and in conjunction with the province.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-GRANT TO NATIVE WOMEN'S ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, along with many women in Canada, was pleased to hear the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) announce this week that the Native Women's Association of Canada will receive a grant of $1,062 million to help in the implementation of Bill C-31.
As my colleagues in the House know, the passage of Bill C-31 ends years of discrimination suffered by many Indian women in Canada, enabling those who were previously struck off the Indian Register to be reinstated to Indian status. Already over 18,000 applications have been received for reinstatement. It is expected that 70,000 to 80,000 native people will be reinstated under the provisions of the Bill.
The grant to the Native Women's Association of Canada will help them inform their members and families of the intent of Bill C-31, and assist them in applying for status and membership. The funds will also enable the Association to monitor the progress and implementation of the Bill, and prepare a report to the parliamentary committee which will review this issue in 1987.
Finally, as these Indian women take their rightful place again in their bands, I know their contribution will have a significant and positive impact on the economic, social, and political progress of all native people.

Mr. Speaker, we are lucky that Thomas Edison did not have to invent the electric light
Oral Questions
under the Conservative Government's research and development policies, for we would still be sitting in the dark.
Unfortunately the science community is being kept in the dark because of the Government's long and inexcusable delay in providing funds for its most important activities. With increasing frequency we learn of Canadian scientists leaving the country for a more favourable R and D climate south of the border. Not a day passes without us receiving dozens, if not hundreds of letters expressing outrage at the Government's failure to recognize that, without funds for research today, we are saying "no" to the jobs of tomorrow.
Perhaps if this dangerous delay is caused by the lack of clout of a junior Minister, we would be better off to absolish the Ministry of Science and Technology and make scientific research and development of responsibility of every member of the Cabinet. Science and technology affect every aspect of our lives. If the Government does not give urgent priority to research funding, we will all end up in the dark, while Mr. Edison's light bulb will illuminate the road to the United States for the most brilliant brains of our country.
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

speechtext: My question is for the same Minister, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: ASSISTANCE TO FARMERS WITHOUT CROP INSURANCE

year.

Oral Questions
suffering the same drought, one with crop insurance and one without, will they receive identical payments on an acreage basis, or will the farmer without coverage receive a supplement?

The House resumed from Tuesday, November 26, consideration of Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections; and Motions No. 4 (Mr. Rodriguez), and No. 5 (Mr. Foster) (p 8837).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-74. It is an important piece of legislation on which I would like to provide some input. Some Opposition Members have left the impression that members of the Conservative Government from northern Ontario have been avoiding the issue. Mr. Speaker, the Member for Nipissing (Mr. Mantha), the Member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Kelleher), the Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais) and I have not been avoiding the issue. We are very pleased to be able to address the issue today.
Since my election in 1982 I have repeatedly dealt with the issue of boundary readjustment. It is an issue which is important to all Members from northern Ontario and one to which northern opposition Members have no special claim. For many years the riding of Timiskaming has been subjected to threats of boundary changes and reorganizations. Since October 12, 1982, the riding of Timiskaming has been continually dealing with boundary changes, redistribution and the numerous problems which it may face due to the realignment of northern Ontario. The situation has been on-going during the three years that I have been the Member of Parliament for Timiskaming.
Before I appeared before the Electoral Boundaries Commission of Ontario in 1983 I contacted nine townships on the outskirts of my riding and 26 within the boundaries of my riding, including the Towns of Onaping Falls, Black River, Matheson, Iroquois Falls and Springer Township. I should mention that the Hon. Member for Nipissing was the reeve of Springer Township at the time. I congratulate him again for now being the Member of Parliament for Nipissing.
I got in touch with the reeve of Chapleau, the Townships of Ratter, Dunnet and Foleyet and the Timiskaming Municipal Association which represents roughly 26 municipalities in Timiskaming. My riding of Timiskaming stretches from James Bay, Moosonee and Moose Factory south to the town of Verner, west to the communities of Matawotchan and Elk Lake and east to the towns of Thorne and Eldee. During the election campaign, Mr. Speaker, when 1 was elected on October 12, 1982, many residents who were included in the riding of Timiskaming in the late 1970s believed that there was no reason for their being in that riding. The boundary change was simply to increase the population in the riding of Timiskaming. I came through with my promise that, if elected in 1982, I would do my utmost to serve the entire riding of Timiskaming. In doing so, I set up constituency offices in the northern and southern parts of my riding in order for everyone to have an input into the problems affecting a riding as large as Timiskaming.
The question of a need for change has been addressed again today. My riding borders on the Ontario Northland Railroad which provides a north-south link between strong community interests that should be maintained. A Member of Parliament must represent his constituents in every way possible. In such a riding, with great distances and sparse population, one's travel commitments make it very difficult to represent one's constituents. Therefore, I believe that this Bill is an adequate response to this problem. Timiskaming his comprised of roughly 77,000 square miles and has a population of approximately 56,000 people.
Let me make some general comments before dealing with Bill C-74. When our Government was elected in September, 1984, it was the first time that northern Ontario had sent four Members from the Conservative Party to represent areas in northern Ontario. It is an area that had never been given the opportunity to maintain and expand its population. During the past 50 years, previous Governments never addressed the

Bill C-74 brings us closer to a fair balance between the ideals of representation by population and regional representation. It ensures that provinces with stable or declining populations will not lose seats or that growing provinces will not be punished. It provides for a simpler distribution formula that is easier to understand.
In addition, I am sure this will be re-evaluated before 1990 and adjusted to fit our future needs. This is an important part of the process which we should not overlook. Furthermore, this formula will slow down the process of an ever-expanding House of Commons. We believe that the quality of representation is just as important as the quantity of representation.
We hope that this Bill will give some stability to the electoral boundary process, which I and my constituents welcome. Bill C-74 ensures that for the first time Members of Parliament will have input into the commission's stages of deliberation in boundary redistribution. At the same time it will provide for a truly independent commission that is free from political pressure.
Many Members have raised concerns about the effect of this Bill. Although we may have different opinions about northern Ontario, I believe we are all concerned about the future of northern Ontario. I believe that the Government is taking the proper action to address this problem.

I would draw upon my own riding, since that is the one I know best, for some example of the effect that will occur if this amendment is not accepted by the Government and incorporated into the legislation.
My riding is slightly larger than Germany, not East Germany, not West Germany, but slightly larger than the whole of Germany. Within that riding sit not a mere 30 or 40 communities but fully 110 communities, of which half are Indian reserve communities.
Right now they are poorly represented.

In that riding, there are some 77,000 people, which places my riding in the very unusual position of having not only the largest area geograpahically, but one of the largest populations in northern Ontario.

I am on my feet today because I believe representation in northern Ontario is a key issue. Despite the fact that there are four Progressive Conservative Members, for example, who represent a combined geographical area and a combined number of communities slightly smaller than the area I represent, I know that representation is an issue for every Member of this House from northern Ontario. Under the present proposal there is no necessity for me to try to protect and advocate the boundaries of my own riding.
We have in the Government's Bill one reasonable objective, namely, to contain the growth and the rate of growth of this House, and another reasonable objective is to contain the costs involved in running the House of Commons.
It goes without question that we could easily augment our Budgets if we would only take the common sense and practical approach of abolishing the Senate. The Senate has never been of the slightest bit of use to northern Ontario, nor will it be for as long as it continues. We know, and even the Progressive Conservative Members know, that in order to represent northern Ontario, you have to do a lot of travelling.
I hark back to the previous Member who represented Timiskaming. 1 recall the gentleman, a dedicated Member who lost his life in a car accident. It was probably because he was too tired to be driving over the distance he was driving. Those are risks, and they are very real risks, that Members from northern Ontario accept. I do not believe that Members from northern Ontario, any of us, need to shoulder an increased load in the representation of our communities by having to spread ourselves even thinner than we do at the moment.
We have a system of distribution in Canada that might politely be described as paying lip service to the idea of representation by population, unfortunately, paying much more service to tradition and history. We have a situation whereby-I say this not to be derogatory-the Province of Prince Edward Island, which could fit into the lakes in my riding, is allowed four Members for a population of 122,000.

In addition, the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act proposes to accommodate the ever-increasing population of our nation, by ensuring that all Canadian citizens will continue to receive fair and equitable treatment in all regions of Canada. The primary purpose of the Act is to prevent unchecked and costly growth in the number of federal ridings across the country. As amended in 1975, the Constitution Act, 1867, provided for the number of Members of Parliament allotted to each province to be adjusted. These adjustments were to be made according to a formula which took into account the

demographic significance of each province, as well as the particular status of the Province of Quebec. Over the years, as a result of these adjustments, an ever-increasing number of Members of Parliament filled the House to near capacity. Under the present formula, the distribution of the increased number of seats, based upon the results of the 1981 census, would increase the number of seats to 310 after the next general election. It has been estimated that direct costs to accommodate extra Members would amount to $90 million.
Application of the present formula would increase the number of Members to 343 by 1991 and to 369 by the year 2001. Needless to say, this will result in a host of problems. It would mean additional administrative costs which would have to be borne by Canadian taxpayers. The physical lay-out of the Chamber is unable to accommodate that number of Members. The significant increase in the number of Members may have an undesirable effect on the character of the House. Private Members would have relatively fewer opportunities and less effectiveness in the House. It has been suggested that the sense of collegiality may suffer. Finally, it is not certain whether an increase in the number of Members in the House would automatically mean that the electorate would be better served. More members does not mean better representation.
The new adjustment formula, as proposed in Bill C-74, while respecting the need for representational equity among the provinces, will slow the rate of growth in the number of Members of Parliament and will thus lessen the operating costs of Parliament.
Let us examine the proposed formula. The draft Bill intends to accomplish three important goals. First, Bill C-74 intends to limit increases in the membership in the House of Commons to levels which are moderate, fair and equitable. Second, the Bill will ensure that no province or Territory will lose seats in the House of Commons through redistribution. Third, it will enable provinces with growing populations to get additional seats in a fashion which reflects the need to maintain the House of Commons at a level close to its present size.
Under the proposed formula, the House would increase to 288 Members after the 1981 census, as compared with 310 Members under the present formula. By 1991, the number of Members in the House would be elevated to 292 as opposed to 343 and, by the year 2001, to 296 as opposed to 369, when I hope to retire as the Member for Nipissing.

This was demonstrated when there was an attempt, which succeeded to a large degree, in the matter of postal zoning for the city, which overlooked the fact that there was a Municipality of North York, Downsview and quite a number of other areas in which people feel that they live in a community and prefer to be identified as such as opposed to simply being a numbered unit inside a pretty large diverse metropolitan area. Thus, this principle is even more strongly applied to the matter of electoral boundaries.
To use my own riding as an example, there are three communities in it which are divided by my present riding boundaries. When the present boundaries were established representations were made to try to draw the boundaries so that the people of a community, for example those people in Downsview, might be able to look to one Member of Parliament in relation to a particular problem which they may have with the federal Government for resolving that problem. When the boundaries do not take account of historic communities that continue to exist in these areas, it tends to undermine the spirit of community which is important in Metro Toronto.
This amendment is one we approve of, but it does not change our minds about the Bill as a whole. However, we will vote for this amendment.

It is good that the commissioners will read the speeches we are making and we hope they will understand the sensitivity and historical background of this country, as well as be very sensitive as regards the notion of community of interests.
Last but not least, it is an old tradition of mine to observe a full census every 10 years, and I am going to go through the fourth census in my career. So I have to be very careful.

In Toronto there has been a switch of population since 1981. There has been immense new development. The same thing has taken place in Montreal. Downtown Montreal is becoming less and less populated, to the benefit of the west of the Island

of Montreal. I am not being political because both extremes of the Island of Montreal are represented by members of the majority Government for the time being. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this redistribution Bill. I want to thank the Hon. Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for moving this particular motion which recommends that in determining reasonable electoral district boundaries the commission shall consider the community of interest and a manageable geographic size.
I come from a part of Saskatchewan where both of these factors must be looked at. The new boundaries that have been established for the Prince Albert constituency contravene both parts of that clause. Neither the community of interest nor the geographic size have been well established in the new map. For example, the proposed Prince Albert constituency takes in well over half and nearly two-thirds of the Province of Saskatchewan. The area is 750 kilometers long and 500 kilometers wide, which makes it an area of unmanageable geographic size.
I appreciate that this amendment gives the commissioners more direction and recognizes a couple of factors which I think must be recognized. If instituted, it will give those groups of people least likely to be heard in the House an opportunity to send a Member to Ottawa who would represent them more directly than is often the case.
I would like to refer specifically to the first part of that clause, the community of interest. In the proposed Prince Albert constituency there are approximately 30,000 people of native ancestry. There is a fairly large but sparsely populated agricultural area which is intermingled with a forestry area. There is, as well, the very small city of Prince Albert with a population of between 30,000 and 40,000, approximately half the total population of the constituency. Therefore, I agree that we should request that the commission review this in the case of the Prince Albert constituency in Saskatchewan. Prince Albert is only one of the constituencies that both of these clauses deal with and I use it as an example because I am familiar with it.
Besides the fact that there may be several different communities of interest in a constituency of that size, the difficulty
in representing such an area should be considered. I have found it very interesting to listen to the debate regarding the difficulty in representing northern Ontario with 11 Members. The area that the Members were concerned about is probably only twice as large as that which is now being proposed for the Prince Albert constituency. Travel, which is necessary to represent a constituency, is very difficult in those circumstances.
I visited most of northern Saskatchewan while I was the director of education for the area. Unless one is to take several months, many places can only be reached by aircraft. Unless the Government starts supplying aircraft to northern Members, they cannot afford to travel to those places. Although the size of the constituency remains large, the number of people can be reduced, which would allow the Member the opportunity to visit more of his constituents in order to gain first-hand knowledge of them. There is a second area which is as large as my present constituency which has a road system and about a third of the population of the total constituency.
Besides that, in this constituency as well as in many others along the northern fringe of the country, knowledge of a number of languages is required in order to do a good job of representation. In the Prince Albert constituency four languages are spoken: Cree, Chipawin, French, and English. The ability to represent communities depends, to some extent, upon the ability to speak the language or the languages of the community.
The basic principle of representation, representation by population, has been honoured by its breach in many places across Canada. I think that situation must be accepted. For instance, at present there are 80,000 people in the proposed constituency of Prince Albert. If we take away the northern area of Prince Albert, which would have a population of over 30,000, that would cause the other smaller constituencies in Saskatchewan to be increased by a population of 3,000 or less. That is not really a major factor as far as an individual Member is concerned. This is true for Churchill and for some other new constituencies as well.
I am suggesting that while the representation by population principle is acceptable and should be a basic principle, we should not consider it as the only way to divide the country. For example, the Hon. Government House Leader represents half of the City of Saskatoon. I believe it would be much easier for him to represent the entire City of Saskatoon than it would be for a Member from Prince Albert to represent more than half of the province. That must be taken into consideration when the boundaries are being drawn up.
It is important that we maintain the fairest representation but that it be not always defined by representation by population.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to speak to Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Bound-
November 29, 1985

aries Readjustment Act. I am particularly pleased to be speaking to Motion No. 6 which deals with the powers of the commission with respect to the definition of electoral district boundaries.
As all Members are aware, it is no easy task for the commission to decide how a particular constituency should be defined and what would be reasonable boundaries. There are many factors which must be taken into consideration.
Motion No. 6 states that the commission shall consider the following in determining reasonable electoral district boundaries. First, the commission can look at the community of interest or community of identity in the historical pattern of an electoral district in the province. The legislation would require the commission to consider certain matters. What does it mean when it says that the commission must consider the community of interest with respect to a particular area? That might present a problem to the commission in the sense that it would have to define first what the community of interest is and then determine how to adjust the boundaries to take that particular community of interest into account.
The motion goes on to say that the commission must consider the community of identity. In my view that might present more difficulties in terms of trying to understand what it means. Does it mean that the commission must consider what particular ethnic group is predominant in a particular area and, in deciding where to draw the boundaries, must the commission try to encompass the whole of a particular ethnic community?
There are arguments for and against that particular suggestion. The argument against it is that it might result in the ghettoization of a particular ethnic community. Some would argue that that is a desirable right, while others would not, but the effect of this motion is to require the commission to look into that particular issue.
Of course, the commission must also look into the historical pattern of that particular electoral district. I do not believe there is any difficulty with the commission doing that in certain areas. In my riding, for example, certain municipalities used to exist but because of changes by the provincial Government through amalgamation and the expansion of particular municipalities, the municipal make-up of Metropolitan Toronto has changed.
A number of years ago we had the old town of Weston that was a distinct municipality in Metropolitan Toronto. There were a number of similar municipalities, the number of which were reduced through amalgamation some years ago. However, the historical feeling of the people in those municipalities has not changed. They still refer to their place of residence as being the Town of Weston, for example, or the Town of Leaside or the Town of Mimico.
It is important that the commission take into account the historical nature of a particular a rea and try to keep it intact as much as possible. We would not want the commission to dissect these historical municipalities that perhaps may no
Representation Act, 1985
longer exist in law but still exist in terms of the feeling of its particular residents.
I represent the riding of York South-Weston. I do not represent the Town of Weston, only the part of it which lies south of Lawrence Avenue, but because the name of my particular riding is York South-Weston, many people outside of my riding believe that I represent them. That is the problem with dissecting particular communities.
The commission would also be mandated by this amendment to consider, in determining reasonable electoral boundaries, a manageable geographic size for districts in sparsely populated, rural or northern regions of the province. We have no difficulty with that particular provision. While the Liberal Opposition supports this particular amendment, we do point out some of the difficulties that might result with respect to the problem of defining or understanding what this particular legislation might mean.
In the few minutes that remain, I would like to speak generally about redistribution. As Canadians know, at present there are 282 seats in the House of Commons. There was a previous proposal to increase the number of seats to 310, an addition of 28 Members. If those Members were Liberal, of course no one on this side of the House would complain. However, all joking aside, the concern raised by a number of Members is that if we continue to use the same formula that at present exists which results in an increase in the House with every census, sooner or later we would run out of room in this place. Perhaps there would be a couple of Members sitting beside you, Mr. Speaker, being able to look at your notes. There would be no more aisles and there would be benches similar to the British House of Commons. I suppose ultimately we might have that program some time down the road when each and every one of us has long gone to other places.
I think there are problems with respect to trying to limit the representation or the number of seats in the House, recognizing the very practical problem of trying to house the extra Members in the House. One has to consider the very basic premise from which we all work, our British parliamentary history that there should be representation by population. That is where you begin. That is a fair place to start. One vote should mean just as much in one area of Canada as it does in another.
We all recognize because of history, and because of our particular history here in Canada, that one has to deviate from the important concept of representation by population to take into account the regions of Canada that are not as densely populated as others.
In the City of Toronto, from where I come, or in any other major city, you do not have the problem of lack of representation in the House of Commons. You do have that problem in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and in other provinces, including Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. These areas are not as densely populated as the larger urban centres. We have to deviate from the principle of representation by

Representation Act, 1985
population to say that in certain areas we will not insist on a certain number of people or on a certain degree of population.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating that my time has expired. It is unfortunate because I wished to raise several other points.
Let me reiterate our position. We support Motion No. 6, notwithstanding some minor difficulties with respect to interpretation that we might have. Generally, though, we are in opposition to the Bill.

Some Members in this Chamber who represent rural areas would say that there should be fewer people in their riding than in a riding considered to be urban. Those Members would say that the urban ridings should have twice as many people in them as in a riding considered rural. If they do not say it they should come clean and be honest about it. Oh, oh!

A name would come up and they would say: "We do not know if that is municipal, provincial or federal". Commons, like the Hon. Member who spoke a few moments ago.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What about the amendment?

The Government House Leader asks about the amendment. As I read the amendment, it is twofold. The amendment which the House Leader introduced says that the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Commission will look at the connection that one part of a riding has with another and will not destroy any historical or traditional links. The second part of the amendment says, "Let us look at geography in the total consideration of the Bill on redistribution."
There is another element coming in here, that is, the type of riding and area that a person represents. I do not wish to make excuses for Members of Parliament but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there are some Members here who sometimes do not know how far to go on a certain problem they get. For example, there are Members of Parliament who are asked to look at an appeal to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, an appeal to the Veterans Allowance Board or an appeal to this or that. Then the constituent says: "We want you to represent us before that board". After that is over, a second appeal comes. Perhaps it is before a court. On one case you are perhaps tied up with two or three days of actual work. You say to yourself, like some Members do who have a 100 or 150 cases of appeals before the Federal Court or the Tax Court of Canada; "Am I really doing justice to these cases?" Some Members are not lawyers. They appear before a judge to get a decision regarding a constituent. I am not saying that there are some Members here who, out of necessity, work ten times harder than other Members. There are certain ridings that require more attention than other ridings simply because of geography and a practically non-existent industrial base.
There is a third element here. Who makes the decision on the third element, I do not know, but it should be taken into account in making decisions on where boundaries lie. In some areas of the country there should be two Members. If this Bill were not before the House, perhaps geographically speaking there would be a separate riding for Labrador. Under this piece of legislation that cannot be so. All it does is to rejuggle the boundaries within the Province of Newfoundland.
I should like to make a point which I think is a very legitimate one. Some Members of Parliament deserve smaller areas of coverage than others, simply because of the circumstances in their ridings. As the House well knows, that determines what is done by a Member of Parliament. I mean, there are only so many hours in a day. A Member of Parliament is
November 29, 1985

either a constituency man or is involved in committee work and everything else in the House of Commons. We cannot do both. That should be a major consideration. In rural areas it is the Members of Parliament who speak on behalf of the people. In other ridings, associations and organizations prepare briefs. Sometimes we do not know one from the other, there is so much representation. However, in rural areas it falls back to Members of Parliament. That should be a third consideration when we are dealing with the particular amendment before the House.
I cannot see anything wrong with the amendment. 1 cannot see any great good coming from it. The reports of the boundaries commission which 1 have read always made the point that an area was a concise geographical one, that one area was connected to another, and used rationale to divide it up. They have always indicated geographic, historic and economic reasons for an area being as it is. However, there is nothing wrong with including that in the actual Act. It certainly re-emphasizes the wishes of the House of Commons. I think we agree with this particular amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to follow the articulations of my colleague from eastern Canada. There are few Members in the House who can approach the Hon. Member's knowledge of electoral ridings, commissions and so on.
I, too, am in favour of the amendment as proposed. However, I have some concern about the English and French versions of the amendment itself in that they seem to give a different perspective. In English the amendment reads:
-the commission shall consider the following in determining reasonable electoral district boundaries:
(i) the community of interest or community of identity in or the historical
pattern of an electoral district in the province,-
The French version identifies the community of interest or the community of identity on a cultural basis as well. That strikes me as being somewhat odd, in the sense that the word "cultural" was not used in the English version but appeared in the French version. I think that is quite significant. It ought to be consistent in both languages, of course, but there is also the importance of the word "cultural". If we are to draw boundary lines based upon cultural group, cultural identity or cultural neighbourhoods within a certain metropolitan or rural area, then I am at odds with such a philosophy. If we base ourselves upon cultural lines, perhaps we are trying to ghettoize something we ought not to ghettoize.
There are a number of different ethnocultural communities in my riding, comprised of Canadians who came from different parts of the world or Canadians whose ancestries were certainly in other parts of the globes. Should we draw a line around a community of predominantly Italian Canadian extraction and another line around a community which may have a Spanish background? I think not. 1 think we must preserve the integrity of communities, whether the delineations be physical or otherwise. However, it disturbs me somewhat that the word "cultural" was included in the French translation of the particular amendment.
Representation Act, 1985
Perhaps we ought to look a litte closer at this particular amendment, to ensure that we will not draft boundary lines based upon culture. Certainly one is a Canadian, whether one is of Canadian Italian background or of Canadian Portugese background. I am somewhat surprised that the word "cultural" entered into the question of boundary guidelines.
In addition, it makes sense to preserve the sense of community in our deliberations. Obviously the legislation will result in new public hearings to solicit support and recommendations from the public at large in terms of where delineations should be drawn. The last series of public hearings conducted by the previous administration were ignored by the present Government. One thing which came through loud and clear in many of those deliberations was the importance which people attached to the sense of community. People were very sensitive to any community being delineated in a way which would perhaps radically change their way of life. Individuals and neighbourhoods came forward, be they businessmen's or ratepayers' associations. Perhaps they were used to doing the community work in their own market areas and being delineated according to those boundaries. They were the last ones to want communities to be cut in half or otherwise. This amendment speaks very boldly and forcefully to the sentiments which were expressed by Canadians from coast to coast. Therefore, it makes sense that the commission be instructed by the House, by parliamentarians, that when it has hearings across the country, these guidelines will be the parameters of the debate. Certainly the debate will be representation by population, but the parameters will be to safeguard what is there now, to safeguard the way of life enjoyed by individuals in their communities. At the same time it should be recognized that we need an equation which will assure Canadians of the best possible representation in the House of Commons.
However, I return to the word "cultural". Perhaps in the ensuing debate, in committee or at the public hearings, that word could be somewhat better defined. As I indicated, it appears in the French version but not in the English version. I do not think we should get into boundary disputes on culture. That is the last thing at which we should look. I am pleased that the House provided me with an opportunity to include my comments in the equation.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, November 28, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reflected upon the capital gains provisions contained in Bill C-84 as I listened to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) trying to explain to the provincial premiers in Halifax yesterday why the federal Government was going to have to change the formula for EPF funding, a change which will result in the provinces receiving $6 billion less over the next number of years for use in hospital funding and post-secondary education funding. The Prime Minister's words were that the money had to come from somewhere; that the federal Government had a big deficit that it had to reduce.
When I heard the Prime Minister talking about that, I could not help thinking about this measure, a measure which will benefit well-off Canadians by allowing them free capital gains appreciation over the next five years up to the tune of $500,000 each.
I have seen a number of assessments as to how much of a drain that represents on the fisc. It struck me that had the Government of Canada been somewhat more rational in approaching the Budget, it would have been possible for the Prime Minister of Canada to maintain whatever goal he has in terms of deficit cutting while still being able to respond positively to the provincial premiers yesterday in terms of their desire to maintain the traditional federal assistance provided to those very important provincial programs.
1 do not think it is digressing at all to talk about the hospital funding programs in Canada. While I was not in the House of Commons at the time, I can recall the kind of encouragement and leadership the Pearson Government provided in convincing the provincial Governments to establish hospitalization programs and eventually to establish universal medicare for all Canadians. Part of the consideration was the promise that the federal Government would be a solid supporter of these programs. Indeed, during the years since-years when there have been largely Liberal Governments in office-the federal Government has stood behind those programs, and it has done so notwithstanding the consequences for the federal financial position. The federal deficit is much larger than it would be had the provinces been left to take care of medicare and hospitalization funding at their expense, as the Constitution provides for programs of that nature. In a spirit of co-operative federalism, the Pearson Government made a strong financial commitment to those programs, a commitment which this
Government is backing away from under the guise of reducing the deficit.
The cost of the proposal in respect of capital gains contained in this measure is one of the principal reasons why this Government is not in a position to support these provincial programs-programs that were undertaken in the 1960s on the understanding, on the basis of the agreement entered into between the Liberal Government of the day and the provinces, that the federal Government would provide transfer payments to assist in their funding.
We do not approve of this capital gains tax exemption of up to $500,000 in one's lifetime. We are going to vote against it. While we agree that the federal Government has to be concerned about the provincial hospitalization and education programs. We in the Liberal Party do not find acceptable the introduction of a shiny new loophole available for the well-to-do in Canadian society while the general tax burden is being increased on lower and middle-income Canadians. That is not something that is acceptable to the Liberal Party, and for that reason we intend to vote against the proposal that there be this capital gains lifetime exemption of $500,000. The Liberal Party does not object to the use of the Income Tax Act to provide certain incentives. Capital gains are already taxed at a lower rate than other forms of gain or income.
I appreciate all of the theoretical arguments that distinguish capital appreciation gains from earned income. However, from the point of view of the morality of it, there is a very good argument in favour of imposing the same rate of income tax on capital gains as applies to earned income. We do not do that in our system because of the incentive that we want to provide for investment. As a result, capital gains are taxed at a lower rate than earned income.
However, this Government is going further. This Government wishes to reintroduce the inequities that the Carter Commission criticized in its report-a report that came out at the end of the 1960s-as a result of which the capital gains tax was first introduced. I very much regret this big opening in the Income Tax Act, an opening which will benefit only that relatively small number of Canadians earning capital gains.
The suggestion made by my leader-a suggestion which I shall repeat-is that we would be more comfortable, if the Government wants to encourage investment by Canadians to see the incentive, the encouragement, focused on the type of economic activity that is truly beneficial to the Canadian economy, the type of activity that creates jobs and economic activity in our country. But, as my leader has pointed out, the way this exemption is drawn, not only does it give tax favoured treatment to the individual who invests to create jobs and to create economic activity, but the same beneficial tax treatment is available to those who buy and sell condominium apartments in Florida or those who buy and sell works of art from the Middle Ages. In other words, any type of investment qualifies for this capital gains tax lifetime exemption, to a maximum of $500,000.
Part of the reason that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) puts forward for going with this much wider exemp-
November 29, 1985

tion than one which we would have been able to support is that he wanted something simple, something that would be easy for taxpayers and investors to understand. To our way of thinking, it would be far better to add a few technicalities to the measure-technicalities which would focus an exemption on encouraging investment of the kind that is useful in job-creation and in building up our country-thereby saving, as some people have estimated it, up to three-quarters of the total cost of this particular tax incentive.
Objective people who have reviewed this proposed exemption have indicated that 75 per cent of its benefit will go to those who make investments that have absolutely no positive impact on the Canadian economy. It is a measure that will encourage the sale of businesses, which is something which may not necessarily be beneficial to the Canadian economy; it will encourage the selling of an apartment in some other part of the world, if one is lucky enough to own one; it will encourage the turning over of works of art.
Can we expect the Canadian taxpayers to support that kind of activity and to view it as something that should receive favourable treatment under the Income Tax Act? We say no. The Prime Minister of Canada, yesterday, said that the federal Government could no longer afford to provide the same level of increased support for hospitalization and medicare, programs administered by the provinces, because of the large deficit. I wonder how many Canadians are going to believe that. I wonder how many will not be able to see that this is done to try to finance some of the mistaken fiscal policies of this Government, including the one before us in this measure.
I want to deal, as well, with the personal individual surtax of 2.5 per cent for incomes of $29,500 to $60,800 and 5 per cent for incomes over $60,800 in 1985. It is pointed out that these rates will double in 1986. Of course, these rates, as much as they are being increased and as much as a surtax is being created, do not result in one additional nickel being paid by those taxpayers who organize their affairs so that they pay no taxes at all. The Government promised in the Budget that it would deal with the situation of Canadians who have high incomes and who pay no income taxes at all. I would like to talk about that problem for a moment.
The reason there are individuals with high incomes who pay no taxes at all is that those individuals have organized their affairs to take advantage of a great many incentive opportunities under the income tax laws which permit individuals to save taxes by making certain kinds of investments and by organizing income receipt opportunities in ways recognized by the Income Tax Act. I recognize that virtually all of those incentives were put in place during the Liberal administration but it certainly was a trend which concerned the former Government and purportedly concerns the present Government. Something should be done about it. No matter what incentives of which an individual wishes to take advantage to reduce his income tax, he should not be able to reduce it below a certain minimum tax.
Income Tax Act
This Government made the promise during the last election campaign that it would introduce a minimum tax so that the situation for which they criticized the Government of which I was a part would be corrected. The temporary individual surtax which the Government has proposed is not the answer. That is not a measure that will increase the taxes of Canadians who pay no taxes at all because of the way they organize their affairs.
When the Budget was introduced, the Minister of Finance indicated that a paper would be introduced and there would be some answer on a minimum tax to be imposed on that category of Canadians by the end of this year. We have yet to see any of the answers. Some of the options have been put forward, but as the end of the year draws nearer and with few days for parliamentary business remaining before Christmas, there is still not a Bill before us to implement that minimum tax.
Another thing that makes this Bill unacceptable to us is that while those who will be paying the minimum tax when it is introduced are free of paying taxes in the meantime, the other provisions of the Budget which increased taxes imposed on ordinary Canadians and reduced the effective amount they receive through family allowances and the old age pensions have already been put into place. They are now beginning to affect the incomes of average and lower-income Canadians.
Whatever Conservative Members said about their constituents and however much they made appeals to lower and middle-income Canadians during the election campaign, what has become clear when looking at their way of organizing the Budget and the way taxes have changed since they have come to office is that the beneficiaries of their policies will be the Canadians who are better off. The people who will bear the burden are the middle and lower-income Canadians. We object to that part of the income tax Bill that is before us and we intend to vote against it as well. I had wished to make some further points, but I will stop now and allow the debate to be taken up by one of my colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House today, to speak to Bill C-84, An Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act.
I am pleased to be able to continue the debate started by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) on November 27, 1985.
The ultimate purpose of this legislation is to restore our country's economic growth and thus provide jobs and enhance the well-being of Canadians. Its purpose is to give each and everyone of us a chance to have a better life and especially to

November 29, 1985
Income Tax Act
give our business people a much-needed stimulus for business development and expansion.
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of Bill C-84 will have the effect of giving our small- and medium-sized businesses, especially, a free rein. They will also give private enterprise the priority it deserves in our country's economy. We have 750,000 small-and medium-sized businesses in this country. We have a million and a half unemployed, a legacy we received from our Liberal predecessors.
As soon as we came to power in September 1984, we tackled the unemployment problem. In November 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented his agenda for economic renewal. Basically, this agenda proposed giving the private sector a free rein and opportunities for profits. It received the confidence of the private sector, which immediately understood, upon reading the agenda for economic renewal, that the new Government would try and save money by cutting Government spending. These measures, in addition to others, should eventually help us to reduce our deficit.
Subsequently, in his May Budget, the Minister of Finance announced to Canadians concrete measures aimed at stimulating economic recovery. Further to this agenda for economic renewal and the May Budget, our Government opened the door to foreign investment by eliminating FIRA and introducing legislation to establish Investment Canada. From now on, instead of pestering foreign investors, we are providing a climate that is attractive for and welcomes investment.
Our Government has also started to dispose of Crown corporations. We will soon be able to announce further significant developments in the disposal process. Canadians will then be in a position to manage, on a profit-making basis, assets which until now were managed by Government technocrats lacking the profit incentive or any other kind of incentive, who moreover were not accountable for their actions, not even to Parliament.
We have also started a very important series of negotiations with our U.S. partners. If these negotiations are conducted successfully, and we intend that should be the case, they will open up a market of 250 million customers, enabling our businesses to become more specialized and to maximize their production processes.
Incidentally, I have the pleasure to inform you, Mr. Speaker, that I have been appointed chairman of a special committee that will regularly monitor and analyze developments in Canada-U.S. negotiations, with special emphasis on the interests of the Province of Quebec.
We also signed the Atlantic Agreement and the Western Agreement. We put an end to the climate of confrontation, the arrogance and the insatiable appetite of the Liberals who were never able to reach a consensus with the provinces concerning the development of Canada's plentiful natural resources.
As promised to the people we have begun deregulating the oil industry. We scrapped the National Energy Program in which the previous Liberal administration had sunk billions of dollars.
Respecting small- and medium-sized businesses, we amended the legislation in order to allow banks to lend them money at preferential rates, and our Government guarantees the repayment of those loans along with the interest. The legislation gives Canadian bankers more operating room and does not create further administrative red tape for small- and mediumsized businesses.
To ease the administration of the act we liberalized a number of significant matters, particularly concerning the caisses populaires which, because of their position, did not enjoy the same privileges as banks did. We lifted some of the restrictions thwarting the business of several caisses populaires so that those institutions, which are well acquainted with promoters and their environment, can now lend them money with the backing of the State.
The Liberals failed to recognize the importance of the caisses populaires.
During the period set aside for questions, the Liberals, unable to analyze the impact of our economic program and envious as they are of our successful efforts have to ask specific questions.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I must also make specific comments. While our Government tells Canadians they may have to put up with some restraints, our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) willingly takes a 15 per cent annual salary cut-back and all Ministers agree to make do with 10 per cent less. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) who is here today happens to be one of those who have accepted a 10 per cent cut in his salary. These are some of the details which the Liberals would rather not mention.
I want to add, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Turner, I think, did not accept to have his salary reduced by 10 per cent. As for Mr. Broadbent, the leader of the socialist party, who is so close to working men and women, to the needy and to widows and orphans, he did not accept to reduce his salary by one cent.
As for the results of our program, they have been extraordinary. We have enabled the creation of over 340,000 new jobs in the last 15 months. The interest rate has gone down by 3.6 per cent. For instance, a smaller business with a debt of $300,000 will save $1,000 in interest costs because of this 3 per cent decrease in the interest rate.
Thanks to these savings, our businesses can reduce their costs and be more competitive on international and American markets, which is very important in this period of intense trade negotiations with our southern neighbors.
November 29, 1985

The lower interest rates on mortgages, securities and lines of credit for smaller businesses will allow them to increase their sales and therefore their production, which means that they will be able to hire more workers.
At the consumer level, a lower interest rate is even more significant if we think about Canadians with a $50,000 mortgage on their home. They will now save $150 in interest costs, and if we consider the impact of the taxation system, at a marginal tax rate of 50 per cent, that is the equivalent of a $3,600 a year pay increase. It is important to point out that a 3.6 per cent decrease in interest rates is the equivalent of a $3,600 a year pay increase for Canadian families.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, unemployment has gone down by 1.3 per cent generally and by 2 per cent among young people.
The Bill proposes measures which have already proven to be effective because of the positive reaction of Canadians. One of the most important and appropriate of these is the capital gains tax exemption of up to $500,000. This provision is economical for the Government because it will not deprive us of more than $600 million in revenue and its positive effects are incalculable.
Mr. Speaker, everyone is sensitive to an increase in his on her assets. The system created under the Liberal Government discouraged the accumulation of assets and therefore prevented businesses from prospering. The proof of this is that the Government had to invent all kinds of public schemes to replace private initiative. Our population had lost all motivation. The possibility of making non-taxable profits thanks to the capital gains provisions will allow our citizens to invest, especially in smaller businesses, and so improve their capital structure and reduce their borrowings.
This Bill also provides for the creation of small business investment corporations, for the purpose, among others, of promoting the provision of venture capital. These corporations will pay no income tax.
Bill C-84 allows Canadians to set up limited partnership investment corporations to deal with small businesses.
The possibilities offered by Bill C-84 will facilitate capital raising for high technology companies. They are the companies of the future, that will be competitive on the North American markets. That, Mr. Speaker, is one way of improving the lot of Canadians.
High technology development used to be done by technocrats in Government laboratories, but as a result of this Bill, private enterprise will be able to generate its own capital and, given the creativity, initiative and fighting spirit of its managers, to develop new technologies directly for its own use.
This Bill also closes some tax loopholes. The objectives set by the Liberal Governments which implemented them could never be reached, due in part to the shrewdness of business people and the lack of foresight of the Liberal legislators. Our
Income Tax Act
Government plugs these tax loopholes while streamlining the Act.
This concludes a few comments on the most important aspects of our legislative program. 1 know very well that the Liberals are going to do their utmost to delay passage and Royal Assent of this Bill. That is the way they work. They have no regard for the priorities of our country. They act on only two fronts. They question minor details and reach a consensus only on the use of filibuster, both in the House and in Standing or Legislative Committees. People should know that Liberals will try anything to delay what we are trying to achieve. That is one reason why they will stay in opposition for a very long time.

We realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a tradition of ghosts leading Prime Ministers. In this case the ghost must have been that of Mr. Mencken and it must have been speaking to our present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The message must have been this: "Young man, if you wish to be Prime Minister, for a short four years"-and perhaps the Prime Minister did not quite pick up that phrase "four years"-"here, Mr. Prime Minister, is the course to follow. It is an easy course, Mr. Prime Minister, a course which recommends itself to me as a humourist in the American tradition. First, Mr. Prime Minister, you tax the middle classes because the middle classes are forever likely to complain and by taxing them at least you give them a target at which to direct their complaints. Tax them seriously, Mr. Prime Minister, because if you do it in a half-hearted way I fear the middle class will not notice because the Canadian middle class tends to be a little comfortable. So tax them and tax them hard."
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, the ghost of Mr. Mencken quoted to the Prime Minister the comments that he made during the Leader's debate when he said he intended to tax the rich and tax them hard. "Then, just to make sure your political future is well established, take taxes away from the rich. Make certain that the taxes you take from the rich are taxes which are completely undeserved. Make certain that the tax breaks that they receive are something that they do not have to earn. Do that and you can be assured of a place in the history books of Canadian politics."
So, Mr. Speaker, a Budget came down with magnificent tax breaks for the rich for which they had to do nothing. They could put their money into the paintings of French impressionists with which I have no quarrel. French impressionism is something I respect. They could put their money into Florida condominiums. Again, I would not want to quarrel with the sunshine of Florida. They could put their money into real estate in Wisconsin. Now, frankly, real estate in Wisconsin is a bit risky in my mind. However, they could put their savings into real estate in Wisconsin and they could receive their capital gains without paying a single penny of tax. We could build up this nice contrast between the poor, hard-working, salaried, middle-class members of our society, whose taxes were increased by this Budget, and the rich with their condominiums in Florida, their investments in Wisconsin, and their French impressionists on the walls.
However, Mr. Speaker, Mencken was not through because the ghost of Mr. Mencken recognized that a full piece of satire had to have its complete exclamation mark. It had to include taking money from the mouths of babes. You could not just tax the middle class and give tax breaks to the rich, you had to also have a system that took from the mouths of children. Then, if you succeeded in putting a package like that together, you could have the ultimate in this country-a tax proposal that infuriates everybody. Therefore, because we believe that Mencker had clearly been listened to, we tested whether there had been this sense of infuriation across the country, thanks to the Conservative's tax measures.
