subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF DEVELOPING PLAN TO REDUCE TOBACCO SMOKING
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF DEVELOPING PLAN TO REDUCE TOBACCO SMOKING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should develop a comprehensive plan to reduce tobacco smoking, its attendant diseases and specifically, that the Government commit itself to discussing co-operative measures with the provinces and introduce the necessary legislation within the coming year.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the House seldom has the opportunity to discuss a matter as important as the one with which we are dealing this afternoon. We seldom have the opportunity to discuss real life and death issues. The issue of tobacco smoking for Canadians is one which affects every person in the country. The problem is very much greater than people realize. As many as 35,000 Canadians die every year as a result of tobacco-related diseases. When we consider that the toll of Canadians in World War II was 45,000 for the entire war, we have some idea of the scope of the problem before us. There are 350,000 deaths in the United States every year and, when we consider the rest of the world, it is into the millions. For Canada, smoking is the number one preventable health problem. Canada is the fourth highest country in the use of tobacco products, and we have the highest rate of tobacco smoking in the industrial world.
Tobacco smoke contains 3,800 chemical compounds, 50 of which are known to be carcinogenic. For some of these compounds, no level of exposure is known to be safe. Sidestream smoke-and that is what we all breathe, whether or not we

November 29, 1985
Tobacco Smoking
smoke and whether or not we like it-contains an estimated 50 times the number of carcinogens in mainstream smoke. We are all badly affected by it. The symptoms of healthy adults exposed to secondary smoke include eye irritation, nasal congestion, headache, cough, sore throat, hoarseness, nausea and loss of appetite. Loss of appetite will become relevant when we consider the level of pollution of VIA Rail. It just may be one of the reasons that the railways company which has the worst food in the world also has the most polluted railway cars in the industrial world.
Twenty-one per cent of Canadians have conditions aggravated from exposure to secondary smoke. This goes from the serious extreme of cystic fibrosis, to the use of contact lenses at the other end. In between, we have people with heart disease, asthma, hay fever and angina, whose lives are indeed troubled by exposure to unwanted tobacco smoke.
Relatively low amounts of carbon monoxide significantly impair driving ability by reducing braking time and by delaying recovery of vision from glare. In short, cigarette smoking causes accidents on the road.
The cost to the economy is estimated at $8 billion. That is the cost in terms of health care costs, medical costs, loss of time at work and fires. A quarter of fire deaths are due to smoking. Only $3 billion is brought in by taxes. In short, we have a $5 billion deficit every year due to tobacco smoking. For a Government which says it is concerned about the deficit, one has to wonder about the $5 billion, year after year, added to the cost to the economy. It is time to act now. All medical associations, including the Canadian Medical Association, provincial groups, physicians, surgeons and the public, are looking to the Government to act.
Prior Liberal Governments failed to act. We can look back to an excellent report of a committee of the House, the "Isabelle" report of 1970. It contained excellent recommendations on how to deal with the problem and excellent documentation. In that time there was the introduction of some Bills, even a Government Bill to ban advertising of smoking in 1971. It was never even debated. That is how much attention the Liberals gave to this most important problem.
Government bodies, such as the Canadian Transport Commission, Air Canada, CN, VIA and all such organizations with federal Government responsibilities, have been given the responsibility to protect the public from tobacco smoke but they do not act. In fact, the Canadian public is exposed to secondary smoke as a result of their failure to act. Not only is the Government failing to act, it is making the problem worse. It continues to encourage the tobacco industry. There is the proposal of a national tobacco marketing board to subsidize exports of Canadian tobacco to Third World countries where the increase in smoking is at the order of 4 per cent per year. It is immoral to continue this. We should be encouraging farmers to switch to other more wholesome crops. Farming is badly hit, in any event, by production in Third World countries. The idea that we should make up for this economic trend by subsidizing exports to Third World countries is flagrantly immoral. Yet, that is what the Conservative Government is considering.
Who, in conscience, can recommend subsidies for a product which is killing 35,000 Canadians per year, as well as people all over the world? According to the President of the Canadian Medical Association, each tobacco farm is indirectly responsible for the deaths of 10 Canadians every year.

We are beginning to recognize the problems of secondary, passive smoke.
Medical authorities estimate that 5,000 Canadians die each year from the inhalation of tobacco smoke pollutants, that is that out of the 35,000 who die each year, 5,000 were nonsmokers. That death rate is five times that caused by driving while intoxicated.
Inhaling tobacco polluted air is equivalent to smoking ten cigarettes a day. I have not even yet raised the ill-effects for pregnant women and their babies, or for children at home. Twice as many children of smokers' families suffer from respiratory diseases as children of nonsmokers' families.
Air polluted by tobacco smoke has become a major problem in the work place. A great many companies allow their staff to smoke on the job even though ventilation is woefully inadequate, with the result that illness strikes employees including nonsmokers, and the public. Customers are also badly served.
Female workers are forced to file complaints through their union representatives. Members of the public and customers have no recourse, nor do non-unionized employees.
Time has come to respect the rights of all Canadian workers to breathe fresh air. Such toxic substances would not be tolerated if they were the by-product of manufacturing processes. They would be banned from the work place, and people would ask for adequate air conditioning devices to get rid of such pollutants.

I have received letters and telephone calls from people recounting the problems they have had at work. People have had to quit their jobs because of the danger to their health. The problem for Canadians who smoke is particularly high because more Canadians are heavy smokers. Therefore, the problem is worse for their non-smoking friends who have to work around them.
The same goes for smoke in airplanes, trains, buses and stations. VIA Rail is the most toxic and most polluted train service in the industrial world. What a record that is! Neither it nor airline companies provide real non-smoking air space. The Department of Transport and the federal Government which are responsible for the unhealthiest treatment of the travelling public in the industrial world are our Government and our Department of Transport. I have written in and complained, as have others. The Railway Act is simply ingored. There is no enforcement. Employees who complain are told that it would cost too much to give them decent air in stations or at their place of work.
November 29, 1985



And the smokers themselves? Both sexes are concerned here since an increasing number of women are now smoking and have fallen victims to this habit. In most cases, today's adults started smoking when the ill effects of cigarettes were not well understood. And the vast majority of smokers, and I mean 90 per cent, would cease smoking but they find it hard to do. We have to help these people quit smoking. The great majority of smokers now admit that smoking is also harmful to nonsmokers. They would endorse stricter regulations if they were introduced in a reasonnable and sympathetic way.
But children are the most pitiful victims of smoking. They now start to smoke when twelve years old. And it is a well known fact that advertising is aimed at the young people, especially at teenagers. One must not forget that the child who starts smoking will be losing, on average, 8 years of his or her life.
Because tobacco companies are losing customers-who quit or die-they are directing their efforts at the young. This is forbidden in their own so-called advertising code, and that code itself is a farce. One tobacco ad agency strategy was leaked to the United States Federal Fair Trade Commission. Let me quote from it. It is very interesting. The following is that agency's recommendation:
An attempt to reach young smokers, starters, should be based upon the following major parameters:
-present the cigarette as one of the few initiations into the adult world;
-present the cigarette as part of the illicit pleasure category of products and
activities;
-create a situation taken from the day-to-day life of the young smoker but, in
an elegant manner, have this situation touch on the basic symbols of the
growing-up process, the maturity process;
-to the best of your ability, considering legal constraints, relate the cigarette to
"pot", wine, and beer.
Altogether, provide starters with a rationalization to start smoking.
And, of course, the cigarette companies are going after women increasingly because men, very sensibly, are quitting in large numbers.
The advertising code is a farce. Complaints do not result in billboards being taken down, even when they are close to schools. Not one billboard respects the provision for a prominent display of the warning against smoking cigarettes. The warning, if you can see it-and sometimes it is hidden behind the lighting-is one to two inches in height. It needs to be six inches in height to be read, and 12 inches in height to be considered prominent.
The warning itself is inadequate. It is voluntary, and the reason for that is that previous Liberal Governments never legislated the warning. The warning is weak. In the United States, for example, the warning says such things as: "Smoking causes lung cancer, heart disease, emphysema, and may complicate pregnancy." In Australia, the warning says: "Smoking is addictive. Smoking kills." That is certainly true. In Iceland, it is: "Protect children from tobacco smoke. Tobac-
Tobacco Smoking
co smoke pollutes the air and is a health hazard." Yet in Canada we have only a very vague warning. It does not mention at all that smoking is addictive; it does not mention at all that it is harmful to children in the family. It suggests that one should "avoid inhaling"; in other words, it is suggesting that the smoker cause more harm to people around him by forcing those people to breathe in secondary smoke.
Fortunately, Canadian athletes are speaking up about the hypocrisy of having tobacco companies sponsor sporting events. The organization Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada counts among its members prominent athletes. They accuse the tobacco industry of "deliberately trying to link cigarettes with sport," and a "flagrant violation of any acceptable standards of corporate or advertising behaviour." I quote:
While tobacco manufacturers continue to pose as exemplary corporate citizens, thousands are dying. These are not good corporate citizens. They are pushers in pinstripes. The fact is that the children are most aware of the brands that do sports sponsorships.
It seems that sport sponsorships are the ideal form of advertising to get young people to start smoking. While adults-especially men-are quitting, young people, especially girls and young women are beginning to smoke. Now more girls smoke than boys, and among young women in their twenties, the percentage who smoke has gone from 36 per cent to 49 per cent in the last three years. It is not uncommon to have 11 and 12-year-olds smoking.
This is shameful and very distressing. The companies are going after young people to get them to start, with the hope that once they get them started, they will not be able to quit. The tobacco companies never admit that smoking is habit forming, that it is addictive; that it will be hard to quit once one starts. They get people hooked when they are young.
Organizations supporting a ban on cigarette advertising include the Canadian Medical Association, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons, the World Health Organization, a number of city councils, a number of boards of education, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Ontario Heart Foundation, and the Canadian Home and School and Parent/Teacher Federation. A report of this House in 1970 recommended a ban, unanimously. A Bill was introduced by the then Minister of Health and Welfare, Mr. Munro, but it was never debated.
Previous Governments have simply capitulated in the face of pressure from the Tobacco companies. It is shameful that the Governments in this country have been prepared to put the interests of the tobacco companies ahead of the health of Canadians. We do not know how much money political parties get from these companies by way of campaign contributions, but certainly that type of consideration has been put ahead of the health of Canadians.
Tobacco companies like to say that a ban on advertising will not make any difference. But we wonder why they are fighting it so hard if they really think that. Let's be very clear: partial bans do not work. Adbvertisers of tobacco products simply shift to other media, as they did when television advertising of tobacco products was stopped in Canada. At that time, they concentrated their advertising efforts on billboards and maga-

November 29, 1985
Tobacco Smoking
zines. In the United Kingdom when tobacco advertising was stopped on the broadcast media, the switch was to gift coupons, various kinds of promotions and giveaways, and sport and cultural promotions. These other avenues of advertisement have proved very effective. As a result, there has not been a ban in actuality. Advertising especially affects young people, as demonstrated by the studies in Britain which show that children smoke the most popular brand. Conversely, where there has been a ban on advertising, as in Norway, the rate of smoking among young people has decreased.
It is an interesting fact that the differences in life expectancy as between women and men are coming together, the reason being that women are increasingly smoking and men are quitting. As a consequence, the life expectancy for men is going up, while at the same time it is going down for women. We have the horrible possibility that we will achieve equality in mortality rates before we achieve equality in any of our economic aspirations or aspirations for political representation.
I am asking the Government to today give a commitment to bring in a comprehensive serious program to deal with this problem. Any such program would have to include a ban on all forms of advertising of tobacco products. Such a ban could be phased in over a two-year period. Along with it, there should be a positive counter-advertising program aimed at discouraging young people from starting to smoke. Secondly, there should be a phasing out of all supports to tobacco production, research and marketing, with those moneys redirected to crop substitution and aid to farmers to get out of tobacco production and into something that would add to the health of Canadians.
There should be legislation to require that there be smoke-free areas in the work place, in places where the public is admitted, and in all modes of transportation under federal jurisdiction. As well, there should be an increase in the taxation of cigarettes, with the moneys so derived directed to counter-advertising, health promotion, research, quitting programs, and crop substitution. In other words, the tax revenues that result from cigarette sales should be utilized in programs aimed at reducing tobacco consumption.

I charge this Government with having neglected the health and the life of Canadians. I charge this Government with yielding to the multinationals of the tobacco industry, with allowing them to make profits out of the health and the lives of men, women and children across the country. On behalf of all Canadians, I call for a realistic and humane program that will stop this butchery.

Mr. Speaker, we have had enough of rhetoric and gesture. This Government has not taken the problem seriously. It is behind Canadian public opinion in that regard. I ask the Government to stop following Canadian public opinion and to start setting it. I ask this Government to do what Canadians are asking, that being to take public health seriously, to take Canada's number one preventable health problem seriously. 1
ask this Government to bring in a comprehensive program which puts the health of Canadians first.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF DEVELOPING PLAN TO REDUCE TOBACCO SMOKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with this opportunity to speak to a subject that is so important to the health of Canadians, and I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for presenting this motion.
As we all know, the Department of National Health and Welfare is aware that tobacco has a very severe impact on the health of Canadians. It is estimated that annually some 33,000 deaths can be attributed to tobacco smoking. Canada is one of the countries in the industrialized world with the highest tobacco consumption per capita, despite a decrease in the percentage of people who smoke, which has slowly dropped to 42 per cent among men and 37 per cent among women. In 1981, this group represented about 40 per cent of Canadians over 14. One item in the figures for 1981 is particularly alarming. In that year, 42.6 per cent of Canadians between the ages of 15 and 24 were smoking 40.5 per cent of Canadian men and, surprisingly, 45 per cent of Canadian women. If we look at the statistical trends for certain illnesses, this could explain why lung cancer is gaining ground and starting to catch up with breast cancer as the form of cancer responsible for the greatest number of deaths among the Canadian female population.
A number of organizations are taking an active interest in tobacco consumption and its effect on health. Programs to deal with the problem have been set up by non-governemental organizations such as the Canadian Medical Association and the Association for Non-Smokers' Rights, as well as by provincial departments of health. As far as the dangers of tobacco smoking are concerned, it seems public awareness is quite significant and increasing rapidly. It is also important to note that society is becoming increasingly reluctant to approve or even tolerate tobacco consumption, not only because of health considerations but also from the esthetic point of view.
Mr. Speaker, the issue becomes really urgent when we consider our young people, who constitute a group that is particularly vulnerable and easily influenced. Is it not true that, often, habits acquired at that age stay with us for the rest of our lives? The consumption of tobacco and other substances that become addictive or create a kind of dependence may result, years later, in the deterioration of our health. We must not forget that tobacco smoking definitely increases the risk of death and also increases the burden on the health care system used by those suffering from tobacco-induced illnesses or a handicap resulting from their condition.
Since the problem can largely be avoided by a change in lifestyle, the Department of National Health and Welfare has both a moral and a legal responsibility in this area. However,
November 29, 1985

there is no easy solution. Tobacco is not an illegal product, and thousands of Canadians depend on the tobacco industry for their livelihood. It has even become a tradition in certain families. It is a fact we cannot ignore when considering measures or programs aimed at reducing tobacco consumption. If tobacco sales were to stop tomorrow, this would trigger a major economic crisis.
In designing relevant programs and to achieve some progress in the area of tobacco consumption, the Department has opted for a specific and methodical approach, using all the resources available to a national federal agency.
In accordance with its mandate by law which is to protect the health of Canadians, the Department of National Health and Welfare directs monitoring programs through its Health Protection Branch. Data on the prevalence of diseases in Canada and their distribution according to age, sex, occupational group and region are collected regularly in co-operation with cancer associations, provincial Health Departments, educational institutions and other federal departments such as Statistics Canada. These data are then transmitted to health care staff and those responsible for health policy, through the medical press, government publications such as "Geographical Distribution of the Death Rate in Canada", conferences and other informative meetings in which the Government takes part.
Such monitoring activities make it possible to establish the incidence of cancer, respiratory ailments and cardiovascular troubles-diseases which strike smokers more than others. After analyzing those data and comparing them with tobacco consumption statistics, we can draw projections not only, to help us draft provincial and federal policies, but also to treat patients, give them advice concerning their specific case, and urge Canadians to adopt a healthier way of life.
The Health Protection Branch also makes tests to establish the toxicological effects of tobacco components. Branch technicians study the genetic effects, analyze the various components of tobacco, and then provide the medical community with their findings.
Since tobacco regulations do not fall within the realm of a specific authority, the DNHW has taken the initiative to come to grips with the health hazards inherent in the use of tobacco. Negotiations with the tobacco industry have been going on for a number of years, more precisely since scientific evidence has shown that tobacco is definitely a health hazard. As a result of those negotiations, a warning appears on all packages of cigarettes, cigars and pipe tobacco. There is full co-operation with respect to grading measures and standardization of lab tests. Technical meetings are also held regularly for researchers of the department and their colleagues in industry.
The industry has agreed to voluntary restrictions to tobacco advertising. A many faceted formula restricts advertising to localities and designs that leave every discretion to consumers.
Tobacco Smoking
This agreement practically precludes all advertising directed at younger people who can be influenced more readily.
In cases where voluntary guidelines might not go far enough, the department takes up the cudgels for Canadians and attempts to convince the industry to change its approach. It must be said that, generally speaking, the tobacco industry has been willing to co-operate with the department on this issue, and that relations between both parties remain positive and friendly.
The department has hired the services of private agencies to come up with advertising campaigns aimed at urging Canadians to smoke less. For instance, in co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association launched an information campaign under the slogan "Pharmacists, Take Position".
In addition, through the Health Protection Branch, the department keeps the public aware through releases on various questions, and responds to regular requests for information from interested groups.
However, the Department of National Health and Welfare is not the only federal department involved in the quest for a solution to the serious problem caused by tobacco consumption. It remains in contact with the other Federal organizations concerned and, under certain circumstances, it takes together with them corrective measures. For instance, the increase in Federal tax on tobacco has resulted in a reduced consumption of this commodity. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the Office of the Auditor General have set up policies to limit smoking in the working place. The Department of National Health and Welfare has just put forward a policy to restrict smoking to specific designated areas identified as "smoking areas". A program is also being offered to encourage civil servants to quite smoking. The Department has adopted this policy on the basis of a survey of its employees who strongly supported the idea of restricting smoking to designated areas. Having consulted a great many people, the Department is now in a position to advise other institutions on the tendencies that emerge and the orientation to give proposed policies in the fight against the use of tobacco. In addition to conducting research on tobacco and providing support to those carried out by various organizations everywhere in this country, the Department subsidizes research in this area through its national program on research and development in the area of health and, indirectly, through the Medical Research Council. That way, the Department is helping channel the efforts of scientific researchers to maximize results.
The Department already has structures allowing it to develop acceptable political options for the purpose of implementing an exhaustive plan to reduce tobacco consumption.
Under the guidance of the Deputy Minister, experts in the Health Protection Branch, the Health Service and Promotion Branch as well as in the Policy Planning and Information

November 29, 1985
Tobacco Smoking
Branch are working together on this problem. The Department can then communicate with the industry, the various Provincial Governments as well as with non-governmental organizations and groups, as well as co-operate with other Departments. Thanks to this organization, the Department has inaugurated major programs like the non-smoking generation and the national program to fight against the use of tobacco.
The Department can rely on the advice of specialists in various areas such as tobacco toxicology, health promotion, clinical medicine, economy, policy planning and legal services. It can focus their efforts toward the finding of solutions to tobacco related problems, while taking into account the impact which these proposed programs are likely to have on the economy of the industry.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has developed guidelines on the use of tobacco for instance in collective transit systems. The Department has also helped other federal agencies and Departments, Crown corporations and private organizations to prepare their own programs.
Finally, the Department provides assistance for outside initiatives in this area, by suggesting for instance anti-smoking guidelines for health facilities and private industry.
Because of the Departmental structure, the Federal-Provincial Community Health Advisory Committee approved in April 1985 the joint development of a national anti-smoking program directed first and foremost at young people, but also at Canadians generally.
The first phase of the program for young people, entitled "For a generation of non-smokers", was launched in October 1985 by the federal Government and provincial and territorial authorities. This is an extension of the "Generation" program of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The federal Government has therefore already shown its commitment to joint initiatives of this type, and constantly explores other avenues of co-operation with the provinces, industry and relevant organizations.
The mechanism for federal-provincial co-operation allows the Department to take on the role of leader in many aspects of the fight against smoking and of the promotion of health. In addition, the Department supports provincial programs which need it and mobilizes considerable human and financial resources to bring Canadians to adopt a healthier lifestyle.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF DEVELOPING PLAN TO REDUCE TOBACCO SMOKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Broad-view-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for bringing to the attention of the House a very important and serious matter.
Needless to say, the ill effects of smoking have to be discussed far more seriously than we have discussed them in the past. It is not a matter of which political Party has done or
not done enough in the past. Collectively, no one has done enough in the past at all levels of Government with respect to this issue. I think we have to be more conscious with respect to the matter. Statistics have demonstrated beyond a shadow of a doubt that smoking is injurious to one's health. Together, as elected officials, we have to give signs of encouragement to those people in the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Minister, and others to increase and strengthen government policies which are now in place in order to encourage our young people never to start smoking and to encourage all others who are still smoking to quit.
Hon. Members know that in its wisdom the Government decided to mount a publicity campaign to encourage people not to smoke. The publicity campaign on television is aimed at young people. It has all types of jingles, music and other things which are meant to tell the young people of Canada that, indeed, they should not start smoking. Of course, that is very laudable. I have watched the ads carefully and they are not quite as convincing as I would like to see them. They do not demonstrate to me the ill effects of smoking. Rather, they portray young people dancing. The idea that you do not have to smoke in order to enjoy yourself is the theme. This is fine. However, we need to have a far stronger message than that for young people.
The other matter with respect to the advertising campaign with which I took exception was the fact that the Government of Canada earlier this month decided to award a contract for an anti-smoking campaign to a company whose claim to fame is the fact that it is the advertising agency for Imperial Tobacco. One wonders about the credibility of the campaign when one considers this fact. Obviously, our young people at whom this advertising is aimed are not fools. They know there is a certain element of hypocrisy in a process which would hire the firm which does advertising for Imperial Tobacco to mount a campaign to tell young people not to smoke.
In my hand I have an editorial dated Thursday, November 14, from one of the Toronto newspapers. It deals with this matter. It is entitled "King size mistake" and states:
At McKim Advertising, they have it both ways. First, the firm is handling more than $6.6 million a year in advertising for Imperial Tobacco, the cigarette manufacturer. And now it has a $800,000 job from the federal government to create an anti-smoking ad campaign.
But we shouldn't worry. Jim Mintz, the federal Health Department's marketing chief, sees no potential conflict of interest. "That was a concern, I might tell you," he told The Star's Martin Cohn this week. "The department and the minister were satisfied that there was no conflict."
That is most assuring. When one reads a little further in the article one will find out why the Minister was so assured. It states:
Why? One explanation is that McKim convinced government officials that it would not play down its anti-smoking ad campaign to avoid offending Imperial Tobacco.
I ask Hon. Members: How on earth can we determine that? First, the company got the contract, which was an untendered contract. Therefore we do not know whether the Government is obtaining the most effective ad which it could for its advertising dollar. As I pointed out earlier, the whole credibili-
November 29, 1985

ty of the advertising process to encourage our young people not to smoke is damaged tremendously by the fact that this company is the advertising agency for Imperial Tobacco. However, there is another thing wrong with the whole process. Let me read further and I am sure you, being a very non-partisan person, will identify it right away. I continue to quote from the editorial:
Another might be that Health Minister Jake Epp is well acquainted with the creative talents of Ron Telpner, McKim's senior vice-president and Winnipeg manager, who has played a key role in Tory election advertising in Epp's home province of Manitoba.
You can see how the Minister was apprised right away of this person's qualifications. The editorial continues:
Telpner denies that he is on the receiving end of a patronage pay-off. "It (the patronage charge) absolutely outrages me," he says.
I can understand how a Conservative getting a Tory job could be outraged by the fact some people are pointing out that he is a Conservative getting a Tory job. Reading further:
Expressions of outrage and perceptions of patronage are one thing; conflict of interest is another. The Health Department has made the wrong choice in McKim and McKim has made a king size mistake in playing both sides of the street on such a controversial issue.
I bring this to your attention because the worst thing we can do is treat the subject of smoking lightly because it is so important. Think of the increase in heart attacks in people who smoke. Think of the lung diseases, some of which are caused entirely by smoking. In other words, we have diseases which would cease to exist if people did not smoke. We are spending countless millions of taxpayers' dollars to eradicate all kinds of diseases, and we are doing so with a certain amount of success. As a nation we have an excellent health care system. I am beginning to wonder whether the Government will put the axe to some of that with the way it is cutting back on transfer payments to the provinces but, be that as it may, by and large we have a good health care system. In recent years that system has assisted in increasing the life span of our citizens. It has worked well. However, if we all got together and really drove home the message of how bad smoking is for our health, if we did it with the serious attention it deserves and in a manner as proposed by the Hon. Member, then we would be a lot further than we are now.
I want to let other Members have a chance to say a few words on this subject, or perhaps we could immediately vote in favour of this good resolution, but I also want to say that I am very concerned about a trend we are seeing now. No doubt the Hon. Member has noticed this herself. We are seeing older Canadians quit smoking and that is very encouraging. In the case of my own family, my mother quit four or five years ago and my father only recently. I am very encouraged by that. However, as I travel throughout my constituency and elsewhere I have been particularly alarmed to see the number of young people who are still smoking, especially the number of young women. I do not have exact statistics on it and perhaps others who are knowledgeable could inform us, but it seems to me there is a shifting between the sexes among younger people
Tobacco Smoking
who smoke. Unfortunately I smoked when I was a teenager. 1 managed to give it up a while back. However, I seem to recall that many young men smoked but few young ladies smoked. Today it seems to me there are as many if not more women smoking than there are men. I know the number of young men smoking has gone down and perhaps that accounts for a portion of it, but it has to be more than that. 1 am convinced that the number of young women smoking is also on the increase. No doubt the reasons for this are peer pressure, the bad example set by adults and so forth. Nevertheless, we should aim the campaign at them in particular because the side effects from smoking are damaging to anyone but particularly to young women. As they get closer to child-bearing age, it is of particular concern because health statistics demonstrate that there is potential harm to the unborn child because of smoking.
I was at a meeting only a few weeks ago in my constituency. One of the moderators was a young woman who was seated beside me and it was quite obvious she was expecting a child in the not too distant future. She was also puffing away at cigarettes. I did not count how many she had during the short meeting of an hour or so but I'm sure it was a half dozen or so. I watched her smoke and the only thing that crossed my mind was why could this person not understand the harm she was doing not only to herself but to the child she was going to bear in the very near future. I am very concerned about that, as I think a lot of Members are. We have to increase the work we are doing there. We have to consider very seriously this motion proposed by the Hon. Member. We should all support it and congratulate her for the work she has done.

I know that the Hon. Member herself opposes smoking, perhaps even with fervour, at least from what I hear, and I do not blame her. It is sometimes difficult for us who have public duties to speak out vigorously against those who smoke, especially when people who come to our offices start smoking. Most of us seem to tolerate this, even if we do not like it. I know, however, that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Green-wood (Ms. McDonald) tolerates it much less than I do, at least according to what I have been told, and I congragulate her on her courageous stand on this issue.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that more should be done in that area. For example, the Hon. Member referred to conditions aboard planes. I admit that some people do smoke, and I do not like it, Mr. Speaker, but still I can put up with it. I seriously wonder why is it necessary to allow smoking aboard a plane travelling between Ottawa and Montreal, a flight of about fifteen minutes.
I am sure smokers can wait 15 minutes to have a smoke, Mr. Speaker. The same thing goes for other flights such as the one between Ottawa and Toronto and other similar ones. On longer flights, if they have to be tolerated, then so be it for the time being, but let us begin somewhere. Let us at least

This is an area where we could implement the suggestions made by the Hon. Member today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH ADVISABILITY OF DEVELOPING PLAN TO REDUCE TOBACCO SMOKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my colleague in expressing my appreciation for the very genuine concerns advanced by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I have experienced the determination that our colleague has just spoken of when she comes into a legislative committee and the first point of order she puts forward is one indicating that she is allergic to cigarette smoke. I do not know whether she is allergic or not, but she finds it offensive and I cannot argue that at all. I respect the concern that she has for her health and that of others. As the chairman of that committee, and a smoker, I do not for a moment object to or feel resentful about that kind of a point of order. 1 am sure that others and other committees will benefit from leaving the weed alone for a period of an hour and a half or two hours while in committee. The Member may be assured that as a health professional I know better, it is just that I have not got to it yet.
The need to reduce tobacco smoking in Canada is an area of concern for the federal Government. Indeed, that is why the federal Government is currently undertaking policies and programs which aim to discourage tobacco consumption and is studying several alternative strategies concerning a whole range of tobacco issues.
As has already been indicated, Canada has a high tobacco consumption rate. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadians smoke. However, polls indicate that the proportion of smokers in Canada is decreasing. For example, in 1985, 41 per cent of men and 37 per cent of women aged 15 and over smoked cigarettes, compared to 60 per cent and 40 per cent respectively in 1966. A source of concern, though, is the rising prevalence of smoking among Canadian youth, especially young women. For example, there has been an increase in daily cigarette smokers among the 12 to 14 and the 18 to 19 year old age groups while smoking among the 15 to 17 year olds has remained fairly constant. Among Canadian women in their twenties, the proportion of daily smokers has increased from 36 per cent in 1983 to 49 per cent in 1985.
There is no doubt that smoking is a major health hazard. It is the single most preventable cause of death and illness in Canada. Over 30,000 premature deaths in Canada per year are attributable to cigarette smoking. It is estimated, for example, that 30 per cent of cancer deaths, 30 per cent of heart disease deaths and 90 per cent of chronic obstructive lung disease deaths are caused by smoking. Male lung cancer
rates are increasing. Lunc cancer rates among women are also increasing and are overtaking breast cancer rates.
I would like to digress for a moment and emphasize what 1 have said in a more real way. Just over a month ago I attended the funeral of a very dear man whom I loved very much; my father-in-law. Up to 16 yeras ago he was a cigarette smoker. I swear that that man of 65 was healthier than I in physique and appearance. Yet, he succumbed to the insidious maglignancy of cancer which first attacked his lungs. He fought that brave battle for close to a year before passing away. To me this has a very close association. It comes even closer when, speaking to my sister a week ago, I found out that the cancer that she as a smoker has been fighting is making further inroads. One can only assume that sometime in the future she will die prematurely. One really must wonder about the sense of myself, as a health professional, being engaged in the same habit. If it is of any solice to those in the House today, I am addressing that problem in a very real sense. Next week I will undergo the treadmill test which will surely tell me that I have been pushing my luck.
To return to the thrust of my speech, economically it is estimated that the monetary cost of tobacco-related deaths and illness exceed the taxes collected and, probably, consumer expenditures on tobacco products. The federal Government is concerned about these human and economic costs and has already put into place policies and programs which aim to reduce these costs. However, the federal Government also recognizes that smoking is, unfortunately, a customary activity with a long history which will be difficult to change. While surveys indicate that smokers do want to quite they, nevertheless, do not want Government to tell them not to smoke. The production and marketing of tobacco has also supported a considerable economic infrastructure ranging from tobacco farmers to tobacco manufacturing employees. It has beena source of employment and income, albeit not the best.
In developing a workable tobacco policy, the federal Government must continue addressing the health problems caused by tobacco smoking while avoiding undue economic disruption to the tobacco farmers and industry workers as the tobacco market inevitably declines. The federal Government has taken an active role in maintaining and initiating policies and programs which will achieve these goals.
I would like to outline to the House some of the accomplishments to date in this regard. On January 25, 1985, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) announced that effective that date all national amateur sport bodies funded in part by the federal Government would be required to desist from any new or renewed sponsorship arrangements with the tobacco products industry for events and programs that primarily involve amateur athletes. The new policy was in response to concerns raised by many Canadians that tobacco products were being promoted through the sponsorship of the Canadian Ski Association by R. J. R. Macdonald Company. This announcement followed extensive consultation with all the Parties involved including representatives of amateur sport governing bodies, the tobacco industry,
November 29, 1985

the medical community and various interest groups. The federal Government decided not to intervene with the CSA-R.J.R. Macdonald contract in order to give the association time to find an alternative sponsor. However, it was agreed by all the parties involved that a formal relationship among the national amateur sport organizations, funded extensively by the federal Government and the tobacco industry, could not continue.
Second, the federal Government has continued to monitor the voluntary agreement among the tobacco manufacturers which has been in place for approximately 15 years. It brings violations of the voluntary tobacco advertising and promotion code to the attention of the Canadian Tobacco Manufacturers Council and holds ongoing discussions with the industry to extend the code. The purpose of the code is the establishment of and compliance with uniform standards of cigarette and cigarette tobacco advertising and promotion in Canada. It has proven useful in restricting cigarette advertising on radio and television and in limiting, to some extent, cigarette advertising
Tobacco Smoking
expenditures. It has also ensured that health warning labels appear on cigarette products and tobacco print, billboard and point-of-sale adversiting.
Third, the federal Government has enhanced its comprehensive smoking prevention and cessation programs aimed at reducing the incidence of smoking in Canada, especially among Canadian youth. It has, through the Department of National Health and Welfare, funded the "Time to Quite" program and the "National Program to Reduce Smoking". The current expenditure level on all non-smoking promotion programs is approximately $1.7 million per year. Mr. Speaker, I see that it is five o'clock and I will so call it.
